Popping Sports Covid Bio-bubbles

By: Julian Sun | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We pop the bio-bubbles that elite sportsmen have been forced to live in

Unique Selling Point:
We look at the mental pressure and the toll taken on elite athletes who've been forced to live inside the bio-bubbles, isolated from family, friends and normal life.

Summary:
one of the most topical stories in sports today is the pressure that comes from living in Bio-secure bubbles due to the COVID Pandemic.

We look at the mental pressure and the toll taken on elite athletes who've been forced to live inside the bio-bubbles, isolated from family, friends and normal life.

The most prominent example currently is the Springbok rugby team. The squad has effectively been isolated from their families, as well as the outside world for the past 4 months. It began in the build-up to the Lions series and lasted 12 weeks when the Boks played their final game of the Rugby Championship. They now come home for a couple of weeks before having to go into another bubble, ahead of their European tour at the end of the year.

Cricket is another sport that has to contend with the effects of bubble life. India cancelled the final test of the series against England citing mental fatigue and this year’s Ashes tour in Australia is under threat due to the unwillingness of the England test team to be away from their families for so long. The Proteas are also impacted. They are currently in a bubble, ahead of the T20 World Cup in the UAE and when they return, they will have to go into another bubble, as they prepare to host India this summer. They too face the prospect of several months living in isolation.

Press Release:


Sports in a Bubble
Playing for a national team like the Springboks or the Proteas means constantly performing in a high-pressure environment, often spending months away from home. So imagine having to do that inside a bio-secure bubble, cut off from a world grappling with the impact of the Covid pandemic. Now, researchers are analysing how these measures are impacting the performance and mental health of some of our top sports stars.
Producer: Julian Sun | Presenter: Masa Kekana

Script:


MASA: COVID-19 has transformed every aspect of our lives, including sports. The only way the games can continue is if sporting teams live in bubbles. These are strict bio-secure environments in which they live in complete isolation for extended periods of time.

V/O: Take the Springboks. After a 20 month hi-atus, the Boks finally returned to the field against the British & Irish Lions in July.

Immediately after, they went to Australia for the Rugby Championship. By the time they played their final test against the All Blacks in October, they’d spent a total of 12 weeks in an unbroken BSE.

SA v ALL BLACKS: (7’45”): These players have not been to their homes since the 3rd of June. They have toiled on this tour, they’ve had heartbreaking defeats…

V/O: Duane Vermeulen plays 8th man for the Springboks

DUANE VERMEULEN (12:21): It’s difficult and people say it’s your job and whatever. It’s not as easy as people think. You’re away from home, you’re away from your families. You don’t see your kids, there a lot of guys whose got children, you don’t spend time with them. That’s vital to your mental state and where you are as a person, as a player.




V/O: Mental coach Paddy Upton worries about the impact of this unnatural existence on performance and mental health

Paddy on the type of pressure that sportsmen are going through.
V/O: Cricket has made extensive use of BSE’s over the last year. Dr Shuaib Manjra is the chief medical officer of Cricket South Africa.

MASA: What is a BSE?

V/O: This year both the Proteas men and women have had to endure the confines of multiple BSE’s. Rassie van der Dussen plays all 3 formats of the game for the Proteas

Talk me through a typical bio-bubble experience from start to finish

V/O: Leg spinner Sune Luus remembers her first bio-bubble

Sune on being trapped inside her hotel room and watching people shopping at a mall.

V/O: The Irene Country Lodge has been used as a BSE on several occasions. It’s a complex logistical challenge to set up according to MD Anwar Karim.

Anwar on why their hotel was chosen and the logistics of transforming the hotel into a BSE

MASA: There’s no doubt that this is a beautiful hotel room that many people would love to stay in, but when you’re confined to this space for days on end, completely shut off from the world, even this luxurious room can start to feel like a gilded cage.

DUANE: It’s a difficult thing being away from home and we had some challenges as a team. The first two weeks were in a hard lockdown, we couldn’t do anything, we had no support in the hotel. You have to do all the things on your own. Make your beds, clean your rooms. It’s a whole different set up out there and then once you’re out of quarantine, it’s a whole different thing as well.

similar comment from Sune

Intercut with a comment from either Paddy or Dr Manjra to support what they are saying.
V/O: Ace spinner Tabraiz Shamsi has spent much of this year in various bio-bubbles and the experience has taken its toll

Tabraiz Shamsi on how busy his year has been and feeling like a circus animal


V/O: International sport is a highly pressured environment at the best of times but is performing at top level sustainable within the suffocating confines of a BSE?

Paddy Upton on the experience of the Chennai Superkings coming last in the IPL because of their BSE experience

Support comments from players on how BSE’s affect performance.

Different players with varying personalities are affected: extroverts v introverts

Tabraiz on his personality changing. So used to being isolated from the outside world that even when he could go outside, he didn’t

V/O: In August, English star Ben Stokes announced he was taking a mental break from the game but do players still trying to establish themselves, have that luxury?

Tabraiz feeling like he has no choice because he has to put food on the table

Rassie on the competition for places within the team and not sure of getting your spot back if you take a break.


V/O: As administrators grapple with the toll that BSEs are taking on players, what is being done to help them cope?

Comments from Dr Majra on sports psychologists being on hand

Contrast with Paddy saying that not enough is being done
